pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–8 (UK Y2–Y3, US Grade 2). Partitioning a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and counting to find the total — the array formalised into a grid, and the direct precursor to area.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y2–Y3 array and repeated-addition work; underpins Y4 area by counting squares.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 2.G.2 'partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of them'; feeds 3.MD.7 (area) and 3.OA (array multiplication).
• Operational details: fill a rectangle completely with equal (same-size) squares in aligned rows and columns, then find the total by rows × columns rather than counting one-by-one — making the array/area structure explicit. Squares must tile with no gaps or overlaps.
• Checkpoint: partition and count by structure. Tier A (7): partition a rectangle into equal squares and count them. Tier B (7–8): find the total using number of rows and number in each row (rows × columns). Tier C (8): explain that the squares must be equal-size with no gaps/overlaps, and connect the grid to a multiplication fact.
bestPractices: Insist the squares are the SAME size and tile the rectangle with no gaps or overlaps — the equal-unit requirement is what makes the count structural (and it underpins area later).
Move children from counting every square one-by-one to using rows × columns, making the array structure of the grid explicit.
Explicitly connect the partitioned rectangle to the array and to a multiplication fact (4 rows of 6 squares = 4×6 = 24) so this is seen as the same structure, not a new one.
Foreshadow area: the count of unit squares that fills the rectangle IS its area — building the bridge to the area topics without yet formalising units.
Use aligned gridlines so rows and columns are unambiguous, avoiding ragged partitions.
keyRepresentations: Rectangle partitioned into a grid of equal unit squares
Rows × columns structure (the array within the grid)
Link to a multiplication fact for the total
commonMisconceptions: Partitioning into unequal squares/pieces (not same-size units).
Leaving gaps or overlapping squares when tiling.
Counting every square one-by-one instead of using rows × columns.
Confusing the number of rows with the number of squares in a row.
Not connecting the grid count to a multiplication fact (treating it as pure counting).

learn.summary: For ages 7–8 (UK Y2–Y3, US Grade 2): partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares, then find the total using rows × columns rather than counting one by one. The equal-unit tiling (no gaps or overlaps) makes the count structural, formalises the array, and builds the bridge to area-by-counting-squares (CCSS 2.G.2 feeding 3.MD.7 and 3.OA; UK Y2–Y3 array work underpinning Y4 area). The central insight is that a tiled rectangle IS an array and its total comes from its structure.

activities.title: Build and read a tiled rectangle grid
feedback: If squares come out different sizes or ragged, first mark ticks the same distance apart along both the length and the width, then rule straight lines through matching ticks so the squares are equal and aligned.

If a learner counts one-by-one, do not insist on the shortcut — model the structural count for the grid they built (e.g. for 4 rows of 6: 'each row has 6; four rows: 6, 12, 18, 24'); the structural count is adopted with exposure.
If rows and columns are muddled (e.g. a 3-row grid called '4 rows of 3'), point along a row and down a column, labelling each dimension before writing the array.
activities.rationale: Varying the grid and contrasting one-by-one counting against rows × columns is intended to let the child discover that structure beats counting; dragging/toggling makes the array concrete as a tiled rectangle. The count toggle and gap/overlap flagging are illustrative interaction examples that make the mechanism visible, not required features.
sourceClaims: 2.G.2 partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of them.
Array and repeated-addition work in Y2–Y3 underpins area by counting squares in Y4; the tiled rectangle is the bridge from array multiplication to area.
learnerActions: Set the number of rows and the number of columns for a rectangle, and watch it fill with same-size squares that snap to a grid; if a partition leaves gaps or overlaps, notice it flagged and correct it so the squares are equal and aligned.
First count the squares one-by-one (slowly), then switch to a rows × columns view and watch the same rectangle resolve to its total instantly — e.g. 4 rows of 6 squares becoming 4×6 = 24.
Write the multiplication fact that matches the grid you built, and say how many squares are in each row and how many rows there are.
Add one more column (or one more row) and predict the new total before revealing it.
activities.intendedInsight: A rectangle tiled with equal squares is a rectangular array; its total comes from rows × columns, not from counting each square, and this square-count is what area will later measure.

activities.title: Partition on paper and count by structure (performance task)
feedback: Prompt with: 'How many squares in each row? How many rows? What multiplication matches your grid? If you added one more column, how many squares then?'
A strong response is a tidy 3-by-4 grid of 12 equal squares, counted as 4 + 4 + 4 or 4, 8, 12 (or 3 × 4) rather than one-by-one, with the grid related to a rectangular array.

Uneven squares, columns that don't align across rows, or one-by-one counting reveal a weak grasp of the array structure — reteach by marking equal ticks first and labelling each dimension; one-by-one counting alone is a developmental stage, not an error to penalise.
activities.rationale: A hands-on partition-and-count task on an actual rectangle elicits independent construction of the grid and surfaces the specific error patterns (ragged/unequal squares, muddled rows/columns, one-by-one counting) that distinguish structural understanding from mere line-drawing.
sourceClaims: 2.G.2 partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of them.
learnerActions: On a given rectangle whose width is 4/3 of its height (e.g. 8 cm wide by 6 cm tall), mark ticks the same distance apart (e.g. every 2 cm) along a long side and a short side, then rule lines through them to divide it into 3 rows and 4 columns of equal-sized squares.
Find the total number of squares and say aloud how you counted — one by one, by repeated addition (4 + 4 + 4), by skip-counting (4, 8, 12), or as 3 × 4.
State which multiplication fact matches your grid.
activities.intendedInsight: Creating equal, aligned squares and then using the row/column structure to count — rather than drawing any lines and tallying singly — is what shows a secure grasp of the array that underlies area.

activities.title: Check the equal-unit requirement and the array link
feedback: If a ragged or overlapping partition is chosen, show that it no longer forms a grid of same-size squares: overlaps get counted twice, gaps get missed, and unequal pieces mean the total is no longer a count of equal units, so rows × columns does not give a fair measure of the rectangle.
If the product is miscalculated, re-count one row, then skip-count by that amount for each row to confirm the total.
activities.rationale: A recognition/matching check reinforces the equal-unit requirement and the grid-to-multiplication link. This format checks whether the structure is recognised; it does not by itself elicit the child constructing a partition, so it is a companion to the construction tasks, not a replacement.
learnerActions: Choose the correctly-tiled rectangle from options that include a ragged or overlapping partition, and say why the equal-size, gap-free one is correct.
Give the total for a shown grid by completing rows × columns = ?.
Match a shown grid to its matching multiplication fact.
activities.intendedInsight: Equal-size squares that tile with no gaps or overlaps are what make the count structural; the grid's total is the product of its rows and columns.

constraints: Squares must be the same size and tile the rectangle with no gaps or overlaps — this equal-unit requirement is what makes the count structural and underpins area.

Do not force the rows × columns shortcut; the structural count is adopted with exposure. A child who partitions correctly but still counts one-by-one has a developmental gap, not an error to penalise.

A static labelled grid (tap-to-reveal rows, columns, total) is a useful reference but cannot let the child vary the grid or contrast counting versus structure, so use it alongside, not instead of, construction tasks.
Recognition/matching items check that the structure is understood but do not elicit independent construction of a partition; pair them with a hands-on partition task.
Keep this planar: volume and 3D packing are a separate later topic and are not part of this objective.

A paper/card rectangle has slight real thickness; treat it as an approximation of the ideal flat figure when discussing the squares as area units, and talk about the mathematical shape represented, not the physical sheet.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The two cited sources are curriculum-standard statements (CCSS 2.G.2 verified:false in the row; UK NC verified:true). They support the learning objective and the array-to-area bridge but do not establish comparative efficacy of any particular activity format.
Arithmetic check of examples: 4 rows of 6 = 24 ✓; 3 × 4 = 12, 4 + 4 + 4 = 12, skip-count 4, 8, 12 ✓; 4 rows of 6 skip-counted 6, 12, 18, 24 ✓. No erroneous distractors were introduced.

Activity 1's one-by-one feedback example is aligned to the activity's 4×6 worked example to avoid a mixed-grid inconsistency; Activity 2 deliberately uses the original 3×4 diagnostic grid, which is internally consistent within that scenario.
Efficacy/discovery wording in rationales is phrased as intended/proposed, since the row's 'moment of insight' design claim is not empirically validated by the cited standards.

The original row claimed dialogue 'adds no unique value' and 3D 'adds no gain'; these categorical modality claims were rescoped to observable limits (planar topic; recognition does not elicit construction) rather than universal laws.

probeDeeper: How did you count the squares — one by one or a quicker way?
How many squares in each row? How many rows?
If you added one more column, how many squares then?
assess.correctAnswer: A tidy 3-by-4 grid of 12 equal squares, counted efficiently as 4 + 4 + 4 or 4, 8, 12 (or 3 × 4) rather than one-by-one — relating the rows-and-columns to a rectangular array.

errorPatterns.pattern: unequal or misaligned partition — rows and columns don't line up, making squares of different sizes or a ragged grid
errorPatterns.nextMove: mark equal ticks along both sides first, then rule lines through them so the squares come out equal and aligned
errorPatterns.revealedBy: uneven squares; columns not aligned across rows

errorPatterns.pattern: counts the squares one by one — tallies all 12 individually instead of using the rows/columns
errorPatterns.nextMove: do NOT insist on the shortcut — model 'each row has 4, three rows: 4, 8, 12'; the structural count is adopted with exposure
errorPatterns.revealedBy: one-by-one counting with no skip-count or repeated addition

errorPatterns.pattern: muddles rows and columns — relates the grid to the wrong array (e.g. calls a 3-row grid '4 rows of 3')
errorPatterns.nextMove: point along a row and down a column, labelling each dimension before writing the array
errorPatterns.revealedBy: the array label doesn't match the grid drawn

responseLevels.gap: Cannot partition into equal aligned squares; the grid is ragged or the squares differ in size.
responseLevels.full: Partitions a rectangle into equal, aligned rows and columns, counts efficiently by rows/skip-counting, and relates the grid to a rectangular array.
responseLevels.partial: Partitions into a correct grid but counts one-by-one, or muddles rows and columns when naming the array.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a rectangle. Divide it into 3 rows and 4 columns of equal-sized squares, then find the total number of squares — and tell me how you counted them. (Watch whether the squares are equal-sized and gap-free, whether rows and columns align, and whether they count by ones or by rows.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Partitioning tests whether the child creates EQUAL, aligned squares (not just any lines) and then uses the row/column structure to count. Uneven partitions, misaligned columns, or one-by-one counting reveal a weak grasp of the array structure that underlies area.
